bearings.paper_claim: Within-politician first-time-donation designs find donations followed by lobbying on the member's bills. Table 1 pooled coefficients 0.041, 0.048, 0.047, 0.023 (SE 0.006-0.007; N 16,434,912 in table, 16,428,834 in text). Matched DiD Senate 0.075 to 0.110 and House 0.086 to 0.127 over t+0 to t+3 (3,778 Senate and 5,497 House instances). Committee-linked PAC lobbying rises 0.103 to 0.147, versus sponsorship 0.029 to 0.037. Lobbying does not predict later donations, except a small sponsor-lobbying term in App K.
bearings.paper_location: Table 1 pp.19-20; text p.20 (2.3 to 4.8 pp, base rate 0.07); Fig.4 and Table J.1 pp.17 and 25-26; Table J.3 p.19 and Fig.5 p.27; App K p.26 and Table K.1
bearings.system_side: Per the analyst: a member-level cross-sectional Spearman-type rank correlation (the code output label says pooled fractional-rank Spearman rho) between member FEC exposure and LobbyView n_bills for 22 lob_ids, with four controls (party, chamber, volume, committee). Raw rho +0.153 and four-control partial -0.0002 were not checked against a results file in this pass. Constants and wording confirmed in fec/lobbying/fec_lda_bridge3_look.py lines 57-80 (CONTROL_NAMES, OVERCONTROL_SENTENCE, UNCORROBORATED wording).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Paper design: firm-politician pair fixed effects, year FE, first-time donation timing, 2008-2018 manufacturing firms. Bridge: member-level cross-section, 2023-26, 22 financial-sector clients, committee control. Different estimand, so the paper does not test the bridge. The paper does not say its committee channel is absorbed by a committee control in a cross-section; that overcontrol reading is the analyst inference (and the code's OVERCONTROL_SENTENCE). The paper is observational and says so (pp.3, 29).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers all reproduced from the text, including the N mismatch. Softened because the claim that the bridge committee control absorbs the paper's channel is an inference, not a paper statement. The rho and partial values for the bridge were not confirmed.

bearings.paper_claim: Outcome is a firm lobbying a bill tied to politician j through sponsorship, co-sponsorship or committee referral, with bills matched by number and title because LDA reports have no member names or unique bill IDs. Bill-linked reports are 0.25M of 1.27M (about 20%) and cover about 97% of lobbying spending. The authors call the estimates a conservative lower bound.
bearings.paper_location: Eq.2 and pp.9-11; text p.10 (1.27M reports, 0.25M bill-linked, 97% of spending, lower-bound wording); fn.5 and fn.9 p.15
bearings.system_side: fec/lobbying/lobby_interactions.py lines 4-5 describe the shipped network as (organization, member, year) counts of whether an organization lobbied a bill the member sponsored or cosponsored. The claim P(joined given lobbied) equals 1 by construction is the analyst gloss and is not stated in those lines.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper uses the same roster join, but its treatment is donation timing, not the join itself, and it treats the outcome as bill involvement, not contact. Neither the paper nor the code supports reading the join as influence or contact (consistent with D-021). The paper's own committee-referral arm is absent from the system's join.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper description verified. The REFUTED label in the analyst output was applied to the system-side rule, not to the paper claim, so it is replaced with a softened reading. The by-construction claim needs a code reference that shows the join.

bearings.paper_claim: Corporate PAC donations show the strongest association with later lobbying of the recipient (committee 0.103 to 0.147 versus CEO 0.017 to 0.050 and employee 0.015 to 0.039). The authors say the estimates should not be read as causal (p.29). The amount effect is small: 0.003 on log donation amount in the firm-politician FE column (Table 1 col.8), which is about 0.03 pp per 10 percent (text p.20).
bearings.paper_location: Fig.5 and Table J.3 p.19 and p.27; Table 1 col.8; text p.20 and p.29
bearings.system_side: fec/engine/flip_model.py line 21 sets WM and WP to 0.35 and 0.65 and comments that money is the minority partner to peer and network influence. Engine money is direct-PAC only (fec/collect/refresh_fec_money.py docstring, individual contributions out of scope).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper says nothing about the WM to WP ratio or roll-call flips. Its outcome is the firm's lobbying behaviour, not the member's vote, in manufacturing firms 2008-2018. It supports at most the general premise that PAC money is the most-associated channel, so it is context and a weak prior, not evidence for the 0.35 weight.
bearings.verifier_note: Relation changed from supports to context. The original code_ref at flip_model.py:17 is a docstring line; the WM and WP assignment is at line 21. The direct-PAC scope is confirmed in refresh_fec_money.py.

bearings.paper_claim: Committee-linked lobbying after a donation is the largest channel and grows over time (PAC 0.103 to 0.147 over t+0 to t+3). Hypothesis H3 predicts the committee channel is strongest (pp.6-8). Committee chairmanship enters the model only as a control.
bearings.paper_location: Hypotheses pp.6-8; Table J.3 p.19; Fig.5 p.27; controls p.18
bearings.system_side: fec/engine/committee_scores.py lines 30-33 and 125-128 set seat base weights Highly 3.0, Moderately 1.8, Slightly 0.9, subcommittee factor 1/6, and leadership multipliers Chair 3.0 full and 7.5 sub, Ranking 2.0 full and 4.5 sub, Vice 1.0 and 2.0. These values match the code.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports only the claim that committee position is where interest-group money and lobbying concentrate. It does not estimate chair, ranking, or subcommittee weights, and it does not estimate committee effects on bill outcomes. Sample is manufacturing firms, federal level, 2008-2018.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claim and the code constants both confirmed. The support is directional only.

bearings.paper_claim: Donor and firm linkage uses constrained graph clustering and fastLink probabilistic record linkage (Enamorado, Fifield and Imai 2019). Executives are classed by SOC 11-1011. The paper reports no precision or recall for its linkage.
bearings.paper_location: Data section pp.11-12; SOC code text at about line 349 of the text file (11-1011 only)
bearings.system_side: C:/Users/pgoff/Mentat/mentat/R/collect.R lines 2110-2156 implement an ordered rule ladder: exact name and same zip gives AUTO, with HIGH if the employer contradicts; exact name and same city gives HIGH; nickname and same zip gives HIGH; nickname and same city gives REVIEW; exact name, same state and similar occupation gives REVIEW; employer contradiction with a name match gives REVIEW; otherwise DISCARD. No name-frequency weighting appears in this ladder.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper confirms the fastLink method and the 11-1011 code only. SOC 27-3030 for government-relations staff is not in the paper text, so that part of the claim is refuted. Suggesting that frequency-weighted fastLink would fix the common-name blind spot is the analyst's opinion, and the paper gives no benchmark. Any change to the ladder is a ruling for Paul under D-040 (not checked here).
bearings.verifier_note: The ladder description matches the code. The SOC 27-3030 attribution is not in the paper. The fastLink improvement is opinion.

related.why: Item title Strategic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying, same authors, same first-time-donation design, an earlier working version of this paper. Confirmed from the item file title and author fields.
The paper cites Kalla and Broockman (2016) at p.4 as the closest field-experiment benchmark on donor access (text lines 68 and 131). Link is real.

The paper cites Huneeus and Kim (2019) on firm-level returns to lobbying at pp.28-29 (text lines 1311 and 79465). The slug year 2018 does not match the cited 2019 publication; the link is real but the year label should be corrected.

summary_issues: Key finding on App D: the item gives 2.6bn of 2.86bn (89%). The paper text says more than $2.8 billion total and $2.6 billion or 89%; the 2.86 figure is not in the paper.

Paper-internal error repeated as fact: App D says 12,862 dyads are less than 0.1% of 5,845,227 possible dyads. 12,862 divided by 5,845,227 is about 0.22%. Quote the count and its denominator, and flag the paper's <0.1% claim as wrong.

Paul's annotation claim (media-blend note that Kim's effects fade within 2 to 3 years; annotation tagged JOP 2026) is not in this item's inputs: paul_entries has no takeaways and the ext record says no annotation file was found. Cannot verify from the item; remove or source it. This version measures rising estimates from t+0 to t+3 and no fade.

Summary says lobbying does not predict later donations. Paper text p.26 says no effects; Table K.1 shows Lobby Sponsor t+0 0.0074 (SE 0.0028) and t+1 0.0041. Say there is one small sponsor-lobbying term at t+0.

Summary calls the CEO and employee links much weaker. Table J.3 has a CEO co-sponsorship value of 0.28 at t+2, far above its row and not discussed in the text. Note the anomaly rather than summarizing it as weak.

Summary says the paper supports the PAC-only scope and the WM less than WP weighting. The paper discusses neither the scope choice nor flip weights; at most it gives context on which channel is most associated.
Paper-internal inconsistency: App G text says the relationship is nonexistent for labor unions while Figure G.1 shows beta 0.6. Note both.

Related links: kept kim-2020-strategic-sequential-links (builds-on), kalla-nd-campaign-contributions-facilitate (complements) and huneeus-2018-effects-firms-lobbying (cites, year to be corrected). Dropped furnas-nd-conflating-lobbying-pacs, bombardini-2020-empirical-models-lobbying, imai-2021-fixed-effects-regression, kim-2018-lobbyview-firm-level, kim-2025-measuring-interest-group and kim-nd-mapping-political-communities: the paper does not cite them, and the same-data and same-method claims about LobbyView and Imai-Kim are not supported by the paper text.

Confirmed without change: Table 1 coefficients and N mismatch; Fig.4 and Table J.1 Senate and House values and instance counts; Table J.3 committee, sponsorship and co-sponsorship values; App D 518 of 9,791 firms, 19,735 of 23,270 donation-only dyads, beta 0.88 and R2 0.39; App L 23 of 66, 17 of 41, 0.067 (+19 percent), 477, 211, 46 and 107 MTB counts; the causal-caution quotes at pp.3 and 29; the 8-11 pp abstract quote; the 82.11 percent supportive figure (fn.12); the 7.8 percent and under-1 percent lobbyist figures (fn.15).

The item key finding that the 0.03 pp per 10 percent amount effect matches only the firm-politician FE column is an inference. 0.003 times ln(1.1) is about 0.03 pp, consistent with col.8; the paper itself does not state which column.

The analyst output shows a 2 to 3 year fade claim in paul_alignment; that is unsupported (see Paul annotation issue above). All bearings and summary claims remain UNVERIFIED agent analysis until a second path reproduces them (DE-062).
